strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and underexplored NLP/CL problem: how VLMs resolve conflicts between visual context and parametric/common-sense knowledge, moving beyond black-box hallucination benchmarks toward internal mechanisms.

The WHOOPS-AHA! construction is well motivated and gives a controlled setting for comparing text-only factual completions with visually grounded counterfactual completions. The paper reports nontrivial scale for this analysis, with 436 LLaVA-NeXT and 432 Gemma3 examples after filtering.

The study combines several complementary analyses: logit-lens localization, head-level modality attention, targeted head interventions, patch attribution, ablation, random-head controls, and comparison to gradient-based attribution. This makes the empirical story more convincing than a purely correlational attention analysis.
Results are reported on two different VLM architectures, and the main qualitative patterns appear consistent across them.

The writing is generally clear, the figures communicate the intended trends, and the limitations section appropriately notes some constraints of logit lens, token-level probing, attention-head focus, and synthetic/curated data.
weaknesses: The causal intervention is underspecified and potentially mathematically problematic. The method says attention weights are modified after softmax with factors such as 1-lambda while experiments use lambda in [-3,3], which can yield negative attention weights and unnormalized attention. It is unclear whether weights are renormalized, clipped, or treated as arbitrary coefficients. This directly affects the validity of the central causal claim.

There is an apparent inconsistency between the formal intervention equations and the prose/figure description of which heads and modalities are boosted or weakened for positive versus negative lambda. This makes reproduction and interpretation of Figure 4 difficult.

The paper appears to select the top factual/counterfactual heads and evaluate interventions on the same dataset. Without held-out examples or cross-validation, the strength and specificity of the discovered heads may be overestimated.

The operationalization of 'internal knowledge' is narrow: text-only preference for a single generated token is treated as factual parametric knowledge. This can conflate linguistic priors, prompt artifacts, dataset biases, and tokenization effects with genuine internal knowledge.

The dataset construction relies heavily on GPT-4o generation and manual verification, but the manuscript gives limited detail about verification protocol, annotator agreement, quality statistics, failure cases, or whether the released data/code are actually available; the code/dataset link appears broken or missing in the PDF text.

The evaluation reduces each example to one factual and one counterfactual first token, which simplifies analysis but weakens claims about generative behavior and multimodal reasoning. Multi-token alternatives and full-generation outcomes are mostly deferred.

The patch attribution results are promising but not rigorously quantified as localization precision. Ablating zeroed visual embeddings is an out-of-distribution intervention, random baselines are weak, and there are no confidence intervals, statistical tests, or human/object-region ground-truth comparisons.

The scope is limited to two models and a curated anomalous-image dataset, so the generality of the claimed mechanism across VLM families, natural images, question-answering settings, or broader conflict types remains uncertain.

Some claims are stronger than the evidence supports, especially that attention from these heads 'pinpoints' conflict-inducing regions and that visual information is passed with 'limited intermediate processing.' The presented analyses suggest this but do not rule out alternative mediation pathways through residual streams, MLPs, or visual encoders.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and timely NLP/CL question: how VLMs arbitrate between visual evidence and internal commonsense knowledge under conflict.
The high-level experimental setup is intuitive, and the WHOOPS-derived examples are well motivated for inducing controlled visual/commonsense contradictions.

The paper attempts to go beyond behavioral evaluation by combining logit-lens analysis, head-level interventions, and image-region ablations, which is a promising direction for multimodal interpretability.
The findings are at least qualitatively coherent across two VLMs, LLaVA-NeXT-7B and Gemma3-12B, and the paper includes some useful controls such as random-head intervention and random-patch ablation.
weaknesses: The central causal claims are not adequately supported. Heads are selected and evaluated on the same dataset, with no held-out validation or robustness analysis, so the reported intervention success may partly reflect overfitting to the selected token pairs and examples.

The intervention is technically underspecified and potentially problematic. The paper says attention weights are multiplied after softmax with lambda in [-3,3], which can imply negative attention weights for some settings unless additional clipping or sign handling is used. It is also unclear whether attention weights are renormalized, making the causal interpretation difficult.

The evaluation is narrow and somewhat circular: factual and counterfactual tokens are chosen based on model probabilities, then the analysis measures whether those same token logits change. This does not establish that full model behavior or generated answers are reliably controlled.

The dataset construction lacks sufficient rigor. GPT-4o-generated captions/tokens are manually verified, but there are no annotation protocols, agreement statistics, quality statistics, or released examples sufficient to assess ambiguity, lexical artifacts, or selection bias.

The attribution claims are overstated. Zeroing visual token embeddings is an out-of-distribution ablation, the gradient baseline is underspecified, and the paper provides little quantitative evidence that highlighted patches correspond to human-validated counterfactual regions rather than generally salient image regions.

The paper relies heavily on Logit Lens despite acknowledging its limitations, but does not use stronger alternatives such as tuned lens, activation patching, causal tracing, or held-out causal mediation checks to validate the mechanistic interpretation.

Reproducibility is weak in the submitted manuscript. The code/dataset link appears as an invalid placeholder, implementation details for interventions and gradients are incomplete, and key choices such as the number of heads, token filtering, and ablation thresholds are not sufficiently documented.

The writing contains several clarity and polish issues, including inconsistent notation, typographical errors, and imprecise terminology such as pixels versus patches. These issues make it harder to verify the methodology.

The contribution is interesting, but in its current form the evidence supports an exploratory observation more than a sound mechanistic account. Substantial methodological tightening would be needed before Findings acceptance.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and relevant problem for NLP/VLM interpretability: how multimodal models arbitrate between visual evidence and learned commonsense/parametric priors under conflict.

The central experimental design is clear and useful: WHOOPS-AHA creates controlled text-only vs image-text contrasts with factual and counterfactual token sets, enabling targeted mechanistic analysis rather than only behavioral evaluation.

The evidence is multi-pronged: logit-lens analyses localize factual/counterfactual tendencies, attention-head interventions produce sizable behavioral shifts in two VLMs, and patch ablations support a causal link between localized visual regions and counterfactual completions.
The paper is generally well motivated, easy to follow, and positioned against relevant work on knowledge conflicts, hallucination benchmarks, and mechanistic interpretability.
Using two distinct VLMs, LLaVA-NeXT-7B and Gemma3-12B, strengthens the claim that the observed late-layer attention-head pattern is not a single-model artifact.
weaknesses: The main limitation is that the empirical setting is narrow: the dataset is derived from WHOOPS synthetic/curated anomalous images, filtered to cases with clear token-level conflicts, so it is unclear how far the mechanisms generalize to natural images, open-ended QA, longer generations, or less artificial conflicts.

The operationalization of internal knowledge is somewhat fragile. Text-only preference for a token is treated as factual/parametric knowledge, but this may conflate language priors, prompt artifacts, token frequency, and GPT-generated candidate-set biases.

The mechanistic claims rely heavily on Logit Lens and on factual/counterfactual token comparisons. The authors acknowledge this approximation, but stronger validation with tuned lens, activation patching, held-out head selection, or other causal mediation analyses would make the localization claim more convincing.

The head intervention appears to select heads and evaluate effects on the same dataset, raising concerns about circularity or overfitting. A train/test split over examples, bootstrapped confidence intervals, or cross-dataset validation would improve rigor.

Reproducibility is only partially supported. The paper mentions code and dataset release, but the visible link is not meaningful, and important implementation details such as exact model checkpoints, preprocessing, tokenization handling, random seeds, manual verification protocol, and intervention normalization are underspecified.

The attribution comparison is promising but limited. Gradient attribution and random ablation are useful baselines, but the paper lacks stronger attribution baselines, quantitative localization ground truth, statistical testing, and enough qualitative examples to fully substantiate the precision claim.

Some intervention details need clarification: multiplying post-softmax attention weights can change normalization unless explicitly renormalized or implemented in a specific way; the paper should specify this because it affects interpretation of causal effects.

The presentation has minor polish issues, including typographical errors and occasional inconsistent terminology, but these do not undermine the main contribution. Overall, I see this as a sound Findings-level paper with borderline main-conference merit rather than a fully decisive Conference recommendation.

strengths: The paper studies an important and relevant NLP/VLM problem: how multimodal models resolve conflicts between visual evidence and internal commonsense knowledge. The framing is clear and well connected to recent work on knowledge conflict and mechanistic interpretability.

The proposed WHOOPS-AHA! setup is well motivated for token-level mechanistic analysis: it provides paired factual and visually counterfactual completions and filters cases where text-only behavior is ambiguous.

The empirical story is coherent across two VLMs. Logit-lens analyses identify late-layer heads with opposing factual/counterfactual preferences, and targeted interventions shift factual accuracy substantially in both directions.

The paper includes useful controls, including random-head interventions, an MLP intervention comparison, a POPE control suggesting the heads are not merely generic visual heads, and a Visual CounterFact generalization experiment.

The attribution analysis is a nice additional contribution: attention from the identified counterfactual heads appears to localize visually anomalous regions better than gradient and random baselines, with both qualitative examples and a small quantitative mask-based evaluation.
weaknesses: The intervention definition is methodologically concerning. Scaling post-softmax attention weights by factors such as 1-lambda with lambda up to 3 can create negative attention weights unless additional implementation details are omitted. This makes the causal interpretation less clean and needs clarification or a more principled intervention.

The dataset validation is not fully convincing. Most quality control relies on LLM-as-a-judge evaluation, while human validation covers only 20 examples with 2 annotators and modest exact agreement for alignment, especially in text-only completions.

The central evaluation uses model-selected tfact and tcofa tokens from candidate sets, which is practical but can entangle the benchmark with each model’s own preferences. This weakens claims about general factual versus counterfactual reasoning beyond the constrained next-token setup.

Reproducibility details are thin. The appendix reports compute and libraries, but not enough exact model checkpoints, preprocessing choices, head lists, seeds, intervention implementation details, or dataset release information; the code/dataset link also appears as a placeholder in the manuscript.

The attribution evaluation is based on only 20 sampled images and SAM-generated masks, so the claim that the heads provide more precise visual attribution than gradient methods is promising but not yet strongly established.

The contribution is sound enough for Findings, but the broader main-conference case is limited by heavy dependence on logit lens approximations, constrained single-token prompts, late-fusion architectures only, and close proximity to recent work on VLM modality conflict and specialized heads.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and timely problem for NLP/CL: how VLMs arbitrate between visual evidence and learned commonsense/parametric priors under cross-modal conflict.
The WHOOPS-AHA! setup is conceptually useful for controlled token-level probing, and the examples make the factual-vs-counterfactual completion task easy to understand.

The empirical story is coherent across two open VLMs: late attention heads correlate with visually grounded counterfactual completions, and targeted interventions produce large directional shifts in the chosen factual/counterfactual token metric.

The paper includes some useful controls, including random-head interventions, an MLP intervention comparison, POPE checks for generic visual processing, and a small transfer experiment on Visual CounterFact.
The writing is mostly clear, and the paper is explicit about some limitations of logit-lens analysis and late-fusion model scope.
weaknesses: The central mechanistic claim is overstated. The evidence shows that modifying selected heads changes a narrow next-token metric, but it does not establish that these heads constitute the model’s conflict-resolution mechanism rather than being highly correlated late-stage conduits or convenient intervention points.

The evaluation is circular in several places: factual and counterfactual target tokens are selected from the same model behaviors being analyzed, heads are identified and intervened on without a clear held-out split, and success is measured primarily on the same constructed contrast. This weakens the causal interpretation substantially.

The intervention is methodologically underspecified and potentially unnatural: attention weights are multiplied after softmax, apparently without a clear renormalization or analysis of distributional side effects. The paper acknowledges output degradation at larger lambda values, but does not convincingly show that improvements reflect selective conflict resolution rather than broad perturbation of late-layer computation.

The dataset validation is weak for the claims made. WHOOPS-AHA! is generated and judged mainly by proprietary LLMs, with only 20 human-validated examples and low exact human/LLM agreement for text-only alignment. This is not enough to support strong claims about commonsense grounding or broad dataset quality.

The notion of 'internal parametric knowledge' is treated too casually. Text-only completions are used as a proxy for internal knowledge, but they may reflect prompt priors, token frequency, or benchmark artifacts rather than stable factual/commonsense representations.

The attribution claim is under-supported. The quantitative mask evaluation uses only 20 images, relies on automatic segmentation, and reports a ratio metric that may be sensitive to object size, patching, and attention normalization. This is insufficient for the strong claim that attention heads localize counterfactual regions more precisely than gradient methods.

The baselines are limited. Random heads and gradients are useful but not enough; the paper should compare against stronger attribution and intervention baselines, held-out head discovery, causal mediation/activation patching, and simpler visual-token attention heuristics.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The appendix gives hardware and library information but not enough implementation detail, exact model checkpoints, seeds, preprocessing, generated dataset artifacts, head lists, or code availability. The first page also appears to contain a placeholder for code/dataset rather than a usable link.

The scope is narrow despite broad language: only two late-fusion/open VLMs are studied, mostly through single-token completion. The paper does not show that the proposed mechanism applies to free-form generation, instruction-following responses, earlier-fusion architectures, or more natural multimodal conflict settings.

Several conclusions use stronger language than the evidence warrants, especially claims that the heads are conflict-specific, mediate the competition, and are not generic visual heads. The POPE result is reassuring but far too narrow to rule out broader visual-processing roles.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and clearly NLP-relevant question: how VLMs arbitrate between parametric commonsense knowledge and contradictory visual evidence. The framing is well motivated and the WHOOPS-AHA! construction gives a useful controlled setting for token-level mechanistic analysis.

The empirical story is coherent and multi-step: the authors first verify that images induce factual-to-counterfactual shifts, then identify polarized attention heads via logit inspection, then perform targeted interventions that causally steer outputs in both directions.

The intervention results are strong across two architectures, with factual accuracy rising substantially under positive intervention and falling under negative intervention; random-head and MLP-intervention controls make the head-specific interpretation more credible.

The paper goes beyond output steering by connecting the identified heads to visual localization. Patch ablation, qualitative examples, and mask-based attribution ratios support the claim that counterfactual heads attend to semantically relevant visual regions.

The authors include several useful robustness checks, including Gemma3 replication, POPE controls arguing that the heads are not generic vision heads, and an additional Visual CounterFact experiment showing nontrivial overlap in identified heads across datasets.
The manuscript is generally clear, well organized, and candid about limitations of logit lens approximations, token-level probing, and focus on late-fusion architectures.
weaknesses: The central head-localization and intervention pipeline appears to select and evaluate heads largely on the same WHOOPS-AHA! examples. Although the Visual CounterFact appendix helps, a clearer train/test split or cross-example validation would strengthen the causal and generalization claims.

Dataset validation is somewhat thin for a benchmark-style contribution. WHOOPS-AHA! is generated and judged mainly with LLMs; human validation covers only 20 examples with modest exact agreement for alignment, especially in the text-only condition.

The attribution evaluation is promising but small: the quantitative mask-based analysis uses only 20 sampled images, and segmentation relies on SAM-3 rather than human-verified masks. This limits confidence in the broader claim that the heads are consistently better visual pointers than gradients.

Reproducibility details are incomplete. The appendix gives hardware, compute, libraries, and prompts, but does not specify enough implementation detail for exact head selection, intervention hooks, preprocessing, random seeds, or full release status; the code/dataset link in the manuscript appears malformed in the extracted PDF.

The interpretation that a small set of heads mediates conflict resolution may be somewhat overstated. The evidence supports effective causal leverage through those heads, but does not fully rule out distributed upstream mechanisms whose signals are merely read out or amplified by late attention heads.

The experimental scope is limited to two late-fusion/open VLMs and mostly single-token completions. This is appropriate for mechanistic control, but it leaves open whether the findings hold for free-form generation, stronger closed models, earlier-fusion architectures, or conflicts involving more abstract knowledge than object/color/anomaly cues.
